text: A sharp hypothesis still needs an experiment capable of actually testing it. On real quantum hardware that's harder than it sounds: the device itself is noisy and drifts over time, so without deliberate controls you can't tell whether a change in your result came from what you changed, or from the hardware changing underneath you.

This lesson covers what a control condition is and why quantum hardware makes controls unusually important, the difference between a baseline and a control, sources of confounding variance specific to quantum experiments — hardware drift, calibration changes, shot noise, and simulator-versus-hardware differences — and why repetition is not optional in this domain.

A baseline is the reference point your result is measured against — no mitigation applied, or the classical algorithm's runtime. A control condition is a run designed specifically to isolate whether your change caused the effect, rather than something else that happened to change at the same time. You can have a baseline without a real control — comparing your result to a number from someone else's paper, run on different hardware months apart, is not a controlled comparison, even though it technically has a baseline.

Real quantum devices recalibrate and drift, so the only comparison you can really trust uses the same hardware and calibration window, the same circuit structure and shot count, run as close together in time as practically possible, with only your one intended variable changed. Concretely: a control group runs the identical circuit with no mitigation, a treatment group runs it with mitigation, you interleave the two across the queue window rather than batching one group first, and you hold circuit structure, qubit count, and shot count fixed across both.

A single run of a quantum circuit is one probabilistic measurement — reporting a result from one shot is like judging a coin's fairness from one flip. Standard practice is many shots, typically hundreds to thousands, to build a probability distribution with quantifiable uncertainty, and often repeating the entire experiment across different queue windows to average out drift. A result reported without a shot count is the same kind of red flag you learned to spot reading other people's papers back in Lesson 2.

Next lesson's lab puts all four lessons together on one concrete scenario — a hypothesis, a controlled design, real illustrative data, and a judgment about whether the result actually supports the claim.
